verses.text: Masters, give to your servants that which is just and equal, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching therein with thanksgiving;
praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds;
that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time.
Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.
All my affairs will be made known to you by Tychicus, the beloved brother, faithful servant, and fellow bondservant in the Lord.
I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that he may know your circumstances and comfort your hearts,
together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is going on here.
Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received commandments, “if he comes to you, receive him”),
and Jesus who is called Justus. These are my only fellow workers for God’s Kingdom who are of the circumcision, men who have been a comfort to me.
Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.
For I testify about him, that he has great zeal for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for those in Hierapolis.
Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas greet you.
Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the assembly that is in his house.
When this letter has been read among you, cause it to be read also in the assembly of the Laodiceans; and that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
Tell Archippus, “Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it.”
The salutation of me, Paul, with my own hand: remember my bonds. Grace be with you. Amen.

footnotes.content: Paul cuts straight to the matter: those in authority answer to a higher Master. I've seen how quickly power corrupts when a person forgets they stand accountable before the throne. Justice and equality in dealing with others isn't kindness—it's obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The phrase 'watchful therein' stays with me: prayer is not daydreaming but alert love, eyes open, grateful heart. I notice how thanksgiving quiets the soul and keeps petition from turning sour.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul asks the church to pray he speaks Christ boldly—not from safety, but from a prison cell. There is something bracing about a man in chains asking others to intercede that he might speak the mystery more plainly still. It teaches where real freedom lives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's desire is to 'reveal it as I ought to speak'—not carelessly or hesitantly, but with the weight and care the mystery of Christ deserves. Even from prison, he thinks about quality of witness, about speaking rightly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Walking in wisdom toward outsiders, redeeming time—Paul knows the world watches believers closely, and time is never wasted unless we waste it. The phrase 'outsiders' reminds us: neighbors, colleagues, strangers mark how we live and speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Grace seasoned with salt: the salt preserves, bites a little, keeps things from spoiling. Good speech isn't honey alone but honest, kind, and pointed enough to matter. I've learned a soft word without backbone does nobody good.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tychicus, the faithful servant and fellow bondservant—Paul names this man with deliberate warmth: beloved, faithful, bonded to Christ alongside Paul himself. These names, each time read aloud to the church, honored a quiet faithful one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul sends Tychicus partly to know their circumstances and comfort their hearts. There's deep pastoral wisdom here: the messenger carries news both ways, and a trusted brother's presence itself is comfort and assurance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Onesimus, 'the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.' This is the runaway slave, now sent back—but Paul calls him faithful and beloved, 'one of you.' That word 'one' erases the old distance; now he belongs to Christ and to the church.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aristarchus, Paul's fellow prisoner, and Mark, cousin of Barnabas—the note about Mark's welcome is real history. Mark had failed Barnabas before, yet here Paul wants him received. That is grace at work: a failed brother restored to fellowship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus called Justus, along with Aristarchus and Mark—'my only fellow workers for God's Kingdom who are of the circumcision.' Paul marks these as few, precious, a comfort to him. When you walk a long road, the faithful ones grow dear beyond measure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Epaphras strives for them in prayer, that they stand perfect and complete in God's will. I notice: he doesn't pray for comfort or ease, but for maturity and wholeness. That's the prayer of a man who loves a people truly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Epaphras has great zeal—Paul testifies to it—for Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis. One man's prayer reaches three churches; his burden for the gospel spreads wide. Such is the reach of a faithful intercessor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Luke, the beloved physician, sends greetings alongside Demas. Luke, who would write the Gospel and Acts, is here part of Paul's circle—and marked beloved. A healer's presence, spiritual and physical, was a gift to the apostle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nymphas and the assembly that meets in his house: I see a living church, gathered not in a grand building but in a home, intimate and real. Every Christian home can be the house of God when Christ is loved there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's letter is to be read in Colossae and also shared with Laodicea; they in turn send their own letter to Colossae. What a picture of the early church: words carried between towns, churches learning from one another, strengthened by shared counsel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tell Archippus to fulfill his ministry received in the Lord. It's a gentle word to a brother who may have grown weary or wandered. Paul knows that sometimes the faithful need reminding that their calling is urgent and true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul writes his own salutation in closing, his hand at work again. 'Remember my bonds'—not for pity, but as witness. Readers today hear an echo in that plea: suffering for Christ's sake speaks louder than comfort ever will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
